text:
Gabriella sat on a small red chair at Miss Penny's music studio. Miss Penny put on a song. "Clap with me," she said. Gabriella clapped. But her claps went fast, fast, fast. Then they stopped. The song kept going without her.

Gabriella frowned. "My claps ran away," she said. Miss Penny smiled. "Try marching," she said. Gabriella stood up. She marched around the room. Stomp, stomp, stomp. Her feet went even, like walking down the hall. The song kept going too. Her feet and the song went together.

"Can you clap like your feet?" asked Miss Penny. Gabriella clapped. Clap, clap, clap. Steady and even. Then she sang, "Baa, baa, black sheep, have you any wool?" She did not stop. She clapped and sang all the way to the end. Miss Penny clapped too. "Again!" said Gabriella.

Maria put on her new hat and went to the backyard. Grandma was at the little grill table. A kettle sat on the grill, and it began to hum. Maria wanted to see the bubbles inside. "Can I look?" she asked.

"Come stand by me," said Grandma. "The steam is hot. We stay back." Maria stood next to Grandma's legs. She held on to Grandma's apron. The kettle went psssss. White steam floated up, up, up. Maria reached out one finger. Grandma caught her hand right away. "Hot," said Grandma. "We stay back."

Maria pulled her hand back. She stayed close to Grandma. They watched the steam together. The kettle began to sing. Grandma put on a big glove and lifted the kettle. Then Grandma poured warm water into a cup. Maria helped wipe the table with a small cloth. "All clean," said Maria. Grandma smiled and patted her new hat. The steam had gone up, up, up, and away.

Bennett ran into the backyard. His dog Buddy was splashing in the little pool. Bennett wanted to jump in too. But the hose had been lying in the sun. Mom held the hose and let water drip on her hand. "Too hot now," she said. "Let it run and cool." Bennett waited on the grass. He patted Buddy's soft ears.

The water ran onto the ground. Bennett put his hand under it. First it felt hot like soup. Then it felt warm like a blanket. Mom put her hand in too. "Now it is just right," she said. Bennett stepped in slowly. The water made his toes feel happy. Buddy shook and water flew everywhere.

"Can we do this again tomorrow?" Bennett asked. Mom laughed and turned off the hose. Bennett waved to the tall fence, where the light of the sun made the water shine. Buddy barked once, and Bennett barked back.

Claire was at Grandma's house. She wanted to make soup for Grandma. She found a small red pot in the toy box. She put in a wooden carrot and a felt pea. Then she found a shiny red berry on the rug. It was not real. It was a pretend berry, made of paper. Claire put the berry near her mouth.

Grandma shook her head fast. "Not in your mouth, sweet pea. That berry is just for pretending." Claire stopped. She looked at the paper berry. She held her pot up high instead.

"Now I will pretend to slurp my soup," said Claire. She tipped the pot to her lips. She made a big slurpy sound. Grandma laughed and clapped. Claire gave the wooden carrot a pretend taste too. "Mmm! It needs a song!" said Grandma. They sang together, and a bird began to fly past the window. It was the last bird of the morning, and it looked in at them. Claire waved her spoon at it. "Soup is ready!" she called.

Declan loved the sand table at daycare. It was warm and soft. It ran through his fingers like sugar.

"I want sand now," said Declan.

"Sand play was yesterday," said Miss Jo. "Today we paint. Sand play comes tomorrow."

Declan had a problem. Tomorrow felt far away. "Where did yesterday go?" he asked.

"It went when you slept," said Miss Jo.

At nap time, Declan lay on his little cot. The blanket was soft. He closed his eyes. He slept.

When he woke up, the room looked different. Miss Jo pointed at the sand table. "Now it is today," she said.

Declan touched the warm sand. It stuck to his fingers. He made a tall sand cake.

"Yesterday I painted," said Declan. "Today is sand!"

"Tomorrow we paint again," said Miss Jo. Declan smiled and patted the cake flat.

Hayden wanted the big blue ball in the library playroom. But the toy box was full of blocks. Too full! Blocks everywhere, blocks on the rug, blocks under the chair.

A girl named Mia started to clean up. "Blocks go in," she said. "Dolls go in. Balls go in." She put in a red block. She put in a sleepy doll. She put in a soft gray elephant. The box got less full.

Then Hayden saw it. When the blocks went in the box, there was room. The loose blocks had made the mess. Now the mess was gone. Hayden picked up the big blue ball. He dropped it in the box, right on top. "Ball goes in!" he said. Mia clapped.

The librarian came over. "The toy box is full," she whispered. "Story time now." Hayden sat down on the big soft rug. He hugged a fluffy pillow that felt like a cloud. The librarian opened a book. Out came a picture of an elephant, and it looked just like the one in the box.

Matteo loved hide-and-seek day at daycare. He found a spot behind the short shelf by the window. He pressed his hands over his eyes. "Now no one can see me," he said.

But Ana walked right up to him. "I see you, Matteo!" she laughed. Matteo peeked through his fingers. Ana was smiling at him. How did she see him? He took his hands away. The room came back. He could see the blocks and the little toy hill on the table. When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you. But Ana still could!

Later, Miss Rosa baked buns in the kitchen. Matteo watched from his chair. He heard the oven door clunk. He smelled warm, sweet bread. He touched his soft sleeve while he waited. Then Miss Rosa gave him a small bun. "Blow on it first," she said. "It is hot, so it could burn your tongue." Matteo blew and blew. He took a little bite. It tasted sweet.

He put his hands over his eyes again. "Can you see me now?" he asked Ana.

"No! You really are hiding," Ana said. Matteo giggled behind his hands.

Adam was at school. It was counting time. Miss Kim sang, "One, two, three, four, five!" Adam clapped along. Then the song went on. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Adam liked the word ten. It felt big in his mouth.

After the song, Adam got paper and crayons. He wanted to write ten. He wrote a big 1. Then he stopped. "Why does ten need one more number?" he asked. Ben sat next to him. Ben showed his paper. Ten had a 1 and a 0, side by side. Adam looked hard. Then he made his own 0. He put it right after his 1. There it was. Ten!

Adam wanted to count real things. He found a fresh green leaf on the table. He counted it. "One," he said. He took a bite of his apple at snack time. Then he counted his crackers. One, two, three, four, five. Miss Kim gave him more. He counted on and on. Six, seven, eight, nine. "One more makes ten," said Adam. Ben laughed and clapped. Adam held up his paper. "Ten! A one and a zero!" he said.

At school, Willow's class was sorting pictures. Miss Beth put out three big boxes. One box was for animals. One box was for toys. One box was for foods. Willow picked up a picture of a bunny. "The bunny goes with animals," she said. She put it in the animal box. Easy!

Then Ben held up a picture of an apple. "This is a fruit," he said. "It goes in the fruit box." But there was no fruit box. Maya shook her head. "No, it's a food," she said. "It goes in the foods box." Ben frowned. Maya frowned too. Willow looked at the apple picture. It was a fruit. It was also a food. It could be both!

"You can put it in two boxes," Willow said. She held up the apple. "Look. Fruit here. Food here. Same apple." Ben smiled. Maya smiled. Miss Beth gave Willow tape, a safe tool for sticking. Willow taped the apple up between two boxes. It hung there, half in each one. "Both are right," said Ben. "Yay!" said Maya.

Juliette loved her soccer team. They played by the big pool. The grass was green and soft.

"Kick the ball to the goal," said Coach Ben. He pointed to the net far away. Juliette ran to the ball. She kicked it hard. But the ball went the wrong way! It rolled toward the tall net behind her.

"Oh no," said Juliette. The ball bumped into the net. The other team did not get a point. Coach Ben ran over. He turned Juliette around with kind hands. "Look this way," he said. "See that net? Kick there."

Juliette looked. The net was far away, by the pool fence. She got the ball again. She looked at the net first. Then she kicked. The ball rolled and rolled. It went into the net! "Goal!" her friends cheered.

Juliette clapped her hands. She kicked the ball the right way now. After the game, they would all stay for dinner by the pool. "I can kick to the net," Juliette told Coach Ben. He smiled and gave her a big thumbs up.

Parker stood by the big blue pool. He wanted to swim like the big kids. Mom held his hand. "You can learn today," she said.

Parker looked up at the tall chair. A lifeguard sat up high. "Why does she sit way up there?" Parker asked. Mom said, "Watch and see."

Parker got in the shallow water. It was cool on his toes. He kicked and kicked. Then he saw a green ball float far away. He tried to chase it. His feet slipped. He went under for a moment.

Splash! The lifeguard blew her whistle. She pointed right at Parker. A helper came fast and lifted him up. "I saw you from up high," the lifeguard said. Parker held the helper's hand. From the tall chair, she could see everyone in the pool.

Parker kicked back to the steps. Mom hugged him. "Swim time is done for now," she said. "Lunch soon."

Parker looked up at the tall chair. He waved at the lifeguard. She waved back and kept watching the water.

Leon wanted to paint a rainbow in the backyard. He looked in his paint box. He found only three pots. "Red," said Leon. "Yellow. Blue." Three pots. Only three. Leon felt sorry for his rainbow.

Then Leon had a big want. He wanted orange for his rainbow. He dipped his brush in red. He tapped it on the paper. He dipped his brush in yellow. He tapped it next to the red. The red and the yellow sank together. The paint turned orange! Leon clapped his hands.

"Orange, orange, orange!" he sang. He painted a big orange stripe. He dipped in yellow. He dipped in blue. Tap, tap. The paint turned green! A green stripe went on the paper.

Red, yellow, blue. Three little pots. Blue and red made purple next. Leon looked at his rainbow. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple. "I made it," said Leon. He held his painting up to the blue, blue sky.

Brooklyn stood at the bus stop with Mom. The wind blew. Brooklyn put her arms in her furry coat. One arm in. One arm out. She tried again. One arm in. One arm in. Both arms were in!

Now the zipper. Brooklyn held the little silver tab. Up, up, up. It stuck. She waited. She tried again. Up, up, up. Click, click, zip! The coat was closed. Mom smiled. "You did it all by yourself."

Yesterday was different. Brooklyn had dropped her coat on the floor. It went under a chair. She looked and looked. She could not find it. "Where is my coat?" she asked. Today she put it on the hook by the door. The hook held it up high.

The bus came. "I can dream of carrots on the bus," said Brooklyn. "Rabbit dreams are the best." Mom laughed. Brooklyn climbed the steps, warm in her zipped coat.

Paisley sat in her car seat. She was going to Grandma's house today. Yesterday they could not go. It rained yesterday. "Grandma has a surprise for you," said Mama. "When?" asked Paisley. "Not now. We drive now. We get there later." Paisley looked out the window. She saw a wild bird fly by. Then the bird made a tree shake. Leaves fell down. One thing made another thing happen. Paisley tapped the window. "Bird, leaf, fall," she said. Mama smiled. "Grandma has baby chicks," said Mama. "One chick came out of its egg this morning." Paisley held up her hand. She counted days on her fingers. "Today, then one, two, three, four, five," she said. She ran out of fingers. "Mama! My hand is not big enough!" "A week has seven days," said Mama. "Use your other hand too." Paisley put up two more fingers. "Seven! I did it!" The car stopped. Grandma opened the door. In her hands was a small yellow chick. "Hello, little one," said Paisley.

Luna ran to the bookmobile. It was a little bus full of books. Dad held her hand.

"I want my own card," said Luna.

The librarian smiled. She made a card with Luna's name. "Pick one book," she said.

Luna picked a book about a red bird. She hugged it tight. "This book is mine forever!"

The librarian shook her head gently. "It has to come back on the due date," she said. "Then another kid can read it too."

Luna frowned. She did not want to move the book from her arms. The shelf looked empty where the red bird book had been.

"Will it be gone forever?" Luna asked.

"No," said Dad. "We bring it back. Then we can take it home again."

On the due day, Luna and Dad went back. Luna gave the librarian the book. She watched the librarian put it on the shelf. The empty spot was full again.

Luna picked it right up. "Hello, red bird," she said. "It's like a gift that comes back."

Athena ran into the backyard. Dad sat on the steps with his tea. "Stay where I can see you," he said. Athena chased a yellow butterfly. It flew past the big grill. The grill was hot and smoking. Dad held up his hand. "Stop there, Athena. Hot things are for grown-ups." Athena stopped. She put her hands behind her back. She watched the smoke curl up. Then she turned around and waved. Dad waved back.

The butterfly flew to the far fence. Athena wanted to follow it. She walked and walked. The tall bushes got in the way. She looked back at the house. She could not see Dad. She could not see the steps. Her tummy felt small and tight. She stood very still and listened. She heard the wind in the leaves. She heard a far-off train. But she could not hear Dad.

Athena called, "Dad!" He called back, "Athena!" His voice came from the steps. She ran toward his voice. The bushes opened up. There was Dad, waving both arms. She ran right into his hug. "I could not see you," she said. "Now you can," said Dad. "Stay where I can see you."

They sat together on the warm steps. Athena counted the butterflies. One, two, three. "That one is neat," said Dad. He pointed to a small blue one. Athena clapped her hands. She stayed close. Dad smiled and drank his tea.

Carter wants to build a big tower at daycare. He finds a heavy box under the toy shelf. He pulls it. He pulls again. The box does not move. It is too heavy.

Miss Ana brings him a light feather pillow instead. Carter picks it up with one hand. It is so light! He puts the pillow on the bottom. Then he adds one block, and another, and another. Slow, slow, slow he goes. The tower grows big.

The tower gets dirty on one side. Carter wipes it with a cloth. Then he puts the light pillow on top. It stays! Carter claps his hands. "My tower is big!" he says. Miss Ana smiles. "Can I knock it down slow?" asks his friend Milo. "No, knock it down fast!" says Carter.

It was Diwali night at Eleanor's house. Grandma set out little clay lamps in a row. "Diyas," said Grandma. Eleanor counted them. "One, two, three, four, five diyas!"

Eleanor wanted them to glow. "Why are they dark?" she asked. "Look," said Grandma. She touched a match to the first diya. A small flame popped up. Then the second diya glowed. Then the third. The dark room turned warm and bright.

Eleanor clapped her hands. The diyas smelled like warm oil. Their light danced on the wall. Papa lit the last two, one and two. "Now all five are shining," said Eleanor. Grandma laughed. "One little flame, one little lamp, one bright night." Eleanor leaned close to look, but she did not touch. She just watched the lights dance.

Brooks stood by the big pool. His swim team was in the water. The coach called, "Time to practice kicking!"

Brooks held the wall and kicked his legs. His kicks made waves. The waves made water splash up. One kick, one splash. Kick, splash. Kick, splash.

"When does the season end?" Brooks asked. Mom had the paper with all the games on it. "We can count," she said. They counted the games left. One, two, three. "Three more games," said Mom. "Then the season is done, all the practices and games from start to end."

After practice, Brooks hid his face in his soft towel. It had white sheep on it, like sheep in a snowy field. He peeked out at the pool. "Three more games," he said. "Then I can kick big splashes at every one."

Paisley stood at the toy shelf at daycare. She wanted to count the cars all by herself. She pointed at the first car. "One," she said. She pointed at the next one. "Two," she said. Then she stopped. She could not remember what came next. Her mouth made a little frown.

Her friend Mia came over. Mia had crumbs on her chin from snack time. "What comes after two?" Paisley asked her. Mia shook her head. "I forgot too," said Mia.

Then Miss Jo began to sing. Her voice was warm like soup. "One, two, buckle my shoe." Paisley heard the words. The two words at the end sounded alike. Shoe rhymed with two. She saw it, like a joke that made her smile.

"Three, four, shut the door," Miss Jo sang. Paisley ran to the little play door and shut it. The click sounded loud. "Five, six, pick up sticks," Miss Jo sang. Paisley picked up a pencil from the floor. It had a sharp point, so she held it carefully and gave it to Miss Jo.

"Seven, eight, lay them straight," sang Miss Jo. Paisley laid the pencils in a neat row. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen," sang Miss Jo. Mia laughed and flapped her arms like wings.

Then Paisley ran back to the cars. She touched each one. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. All the words came out in a line now. Mia clapped her hands.

"Sing it again," said Mia. So they sang together, all the way to ten.

Clara went to the community centre with her dad. The room had small tables and many toys. A big bell sat by the door. When it was time to start, a teacher rang the bell, and the children came to sit down. There was a boy there named Sam. He had a toy car in his hand.

The teacher put out two bowls of crackers. She asked, "Which bowl has more?" Clara pointed at the tall pile in the red bowl. The teacher said, "Let's count and see." Clara touched each cracker. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." The red bowl had more.

Clara wanted to eat a cracker. She took one from the red bowl. Then she counted again. "One, two, three, four." Now Sam counted the blue bowl. "One, two, three." Clara said, "Mine still has more!" Sam laughed. He took one from the blue bowl too. Clara counted his bowl. "One, two."

Sam pushed his toy car across the table. "Now you have more than me," he said. Clara slid two crackers to his bowl. She counted both bowls. "Four and four. The same!" Sam clapped his hands.

The teacher rang the bell again. It was time for juice. Clara held Sam's hand, and they walked to the little cups together. "You can sit by me," said Clara. Sam rolled his car along beside her, all the way to the snack table.

Eliana sat in the car with her mama. They were going to the dentist. "My first time," said Eliana. Her tummy felt funny. Was she hungry? No. She had eaten breakfast.

The car stopped. They went in together. A big chair sat in the middle of the room. "Sit here," said the dentist. Eliana climbed up. Then a bright light glowed over her head. Eliana closed her eyes. It was too bright!

"Here," said the dentist. She gave Eliana little sunglasses. Eliana put them on. Now her eyes felt good. She opened her mouth wide. The light shone in. The dentist looked and looked. "I can see all your teeth," she said.

Eliana wondered. Did the light help the dentist see? She tried closing her mouth. The dentist could not see anymore. She opened it again. The light went in. The dentist smiled and counted every tooth. "Nice and clean," she said.

In the car, Eliana held her new toothbrush. "Mama," she said, "the light was so bright, but my sunglasses helped." She looked out the window. "Can the sun wear sunglasses too?"

Sofia held her red backpack tight. It was her first day of school. She walked down the big hallway with her mama. The floor was shiny. "I wonder how many doors there are," Sofia said. She counted one, two, three.

Then Sofia saw her friend Ben. Ben had been on the school bus that morning. "I stood up on the bus," Ben said. "I wanted to wave out the window at the sheep in the field." The sheep had white wool and stood by a red barn.

"What happened when you stood up?" Sofia asked. "The driver asked me to sit down," Ben said. "So I sat in my seat the whole way." Sofia nodded. "On the bus, we stay sitting in our seats," she said.

A teacher came to the door. "Time to mix the paint for our art table," she said. Sofia and Ben ran to the red table. Sofia picked up a brush. "I will paint the sheep by the barn," she said.

Jordan planted seeds in the school garden. He made a deep little hole for each one. Then he patted the soil on top. "Grow, little seeds," he said.

Every morning Jordan ran to the garden. He saw a carrot patch. Maya's seeds had green shoots. Ben's seeds had green shoots. Jordan's pot had nothing at all. Just brown dirt. Jordan sat down in the circle of friends. He did not want to share his sad face.

Then he saw Maya hold her watering can. She tipped it over her shoots. Drip, drip, drip. Jordan touched his soil. It was dry and crumbly. He had never given his seeds any water. Jordan found his own little can. He filled it at the tap. He poured the water slowly and softly over the dirt.

The next morning, Jordan tiptoed to the pot. A tiny green shoot was peeking out. It had a little white hat of seed shell on top. Jordan clapped his hands. "Hello, little plant!" he called. Maya peeked over and smiled. "Mine did that too," she said. Jordan held up his watering can with both hands. "Water time," he said.

Mila wanted to find her red sock. It was lost somewhere in the playroom. She looked under the big teddy bear. Not there. She looked in the small toy box. Not there.

Then she saw her dog, Max, by the door. His tail was wagging fast. "Do you know where my sock is?" she asked. Max wagged his tail slow and happy. He was sitting on something. It was the red sock! But the sock was wet. Max had dripped water on it from his walk. "Wet sock," said Mila with a sigh. "I need a dry one."

Mila put the wet sock on the warm radiator. Mom helped her stay far from it, because it was hot. Then Mila found a dry blue sock in her drawer. She put it on her small foot. Max licked her toe, fast then slow. "Good boy," said Mila. "Now my foot is dry, and my sock is not!" She patted his soft ear, and they sat together on the rug.

Luca ran to the backyard. His ball was lost! He wanted to find it before bed.

He looked by the red flowers. He looked by the green grass. He looked up at the blue sky. No ball. Then he heard a bump. The yellow ball rolled out from under a bush. "I found it!" he shouted.

At bedtime, Luca picked socks in his dark room. He could not tell what color they were. He put them on and jumped into bed.

In the morning, the sun came in. Luca looked down. One sock was red. One sock was green. He laughed and laughed. "Silly socks!" he said. He ran outside with the yellow ball, happy to see all the colors in the light.

Elijah went to the ice rink with Mom and his friend Sam. They skated on the fresh ice until their toes were cold. Then they sat on a bench with hot cocoa. A big soccer game was on the TV by the snack bar.

Elijah watched a player run with the ball. The player kicked it high. The ball went up over the net. The crowd made a sad sound. "He missed," said Sam.

Elijah kept watching. He waited a long time. Another player ran fast. She kicked the ball low. The ball rolled along the ground. It went right into the net. The crowd jumped up and cheered.

The goal! Elijah stood on the bench and waved his arms. "The ball went in!" he said. Sam kissed his own hand and patted the screen. Mom laughed. A new player got the ball. Elijah sat very still and watched. His eyes followed the ball the whole way. It went into the net again. "Goal!" said Elijah.

Margot sat on her big bed. Her friend Noa had given her a book from daycare. It had a dog on the cover and funny letters inside.

Margot opened the book from the left side. She peeked at a page. "That looks like a stinky sock," she giggled. "Dog, where are you?" The dog was not there. Margot pouted. She sank down into her pillows.

Then Noa's voice popped into her head. "My book opens the other way." Margot turned the book around. She opened it from the right side. There was the dog! "One page, two pages, three!" she said. The dog ran and ran.

Margot grabbed her crayon. She made her own dog on paper. "My dog goes this way," she said. "Your dog goes that way."

"Papa! Look at Noa's funny book!"

Sophie sat in the car. She sat in her deep blue seat. Mom sat in front with the new baby. The baby was wrapped in a soft blanket.

"I miss you, Mom," Sophie said. "Just you and me."

Mom looked back at Sophie. "I hear you," Mom said. "That is okay to feel."

Sophie counted the cars going by. One car. Two cars. Three cars. The baby began to cry. Mom sang to him. Then Mom sang to Sophie too. Sophie sang along. The baby stopped crying.

At home, Dad gave Sophie a cookie. Mom put the baby in his bed. Then Mom sat next to Sophie. Just Mom and Sophie, eating one cookie together.

"Again tomorrow?" Mom asked.

"Yes," said Sophie. "Cookie for two."

Axel sat at the dinner table. He wanted pancakes. Daddy made pancakes on Saturday. "How many days until Saturday?" Axel asked.

Mommy held up her hand. "Count with me," she said. Axel tapped her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Seven fingers. Seven days in one week.

Axel counted again. He poked each finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six." He stopped. One finger was still down. That finger was Saturday! "Six more days, then Saturday!" he shouted.

Axel ran to the calendar. He made a mark on today. Tomorrow he would make another mark. He counted all the marks. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" A whole week on the wall.

At dinner, Axel told his baby sister. "Pancakes on Saturday!" She smiled. One tooth was missing on the bottom. She clapped her hands. Daddy said, "I will not forget the pancakes." Axel ate his peas fast. He made one more mark on the calendar before bed.

Joshua ran into the school cooking classroom. Today he would make bread for his family! "I will stir the mix," he said. Teacher Mia smiled. Joshua counted the cups, one, two, three. He poured them in. He stirred and stirred. The mix looked like soft mud.

Next came the butter. Joshua opened the little fridge. He took out the butter. It was cold and hard. He pushed it with his spoon. The butter would not spread. It sat on the bread like a hard little rock. "Oh no," said Joshua. "My bread!"

Teacher Mia put the butter on the counter. "We will wait a bit," she said. Joshua waited. He tapped his spoon, one, two, three. Then he touched the butter. It felt soft now! He spread it on the warm bread. The butter went smooth and shiny. "Soft butter, happy bread, happy family!" Joshua carried the plate to the door. "Look what I made!"

Benjamin was playing house at daycare. He was the daddy. His friend Mia was the mommy. They had a baby made from a sock.

Then Benjamin dropped the baby sock. It fell on the floor. Mia looked sad. "The baby fell!" she said. Her lip wobbled.

Teacher Ana came over. She picked up the sock. "Look," she said softly. "The sock baby is fine. Socks cannot get hurt." She held it out. "But you can give it a pretend hug."

Benjamin took the sock. He hugged it tight. He rocked it back and forth. "There, there, baby," he said in a small voice. Mia wiped her eyes. Then she laughed.

"Shh, the baby is sleeping," Benjamin whispered. He put the sock on a little bed of blocks. Mia put a tiny blanket on top. It was just a paper napkin, but it looked soft like snow on a mountain.

The baby slept and slept. Benjamin patted it gently. "Time to eat," he said. He held a pretend bottle to the sock. "Mmm," he said.

Then the sock rolled right off the bed! Benjamin grabbed it fast. "I caught you!" he said. He was scared for one second, but then he smiled. The sock could not really be hurt. So he kissed its head and held it close.

"Again, again!" laughed Mia. So Benjamin dropped it, and caught it, and hugged it every time.

Milan loved the school library. On Tuesday his teacher said, "Yesterday we read about bears. Tomorrow we will go to the library."

Milan could not wait. He wanted the bright red book about trucks.

On Wednesday morning, Milan asked his friend Sam, "Is today the library day?"

Sam said, "I don't know."

Milan asked his teacher. She smiled and said, "Yes. Today is the day. It is happening right now."

Milan jumped up and down. "Now?" he asked.

"Now," said the teacher. "But first we will cook bread in the kitchen. The library comes later."

Milan waited. He stirred the flour. He watched the teacher put the pan in the oven, because the oven was hot. The bread smelled good.

"Now is it later?" Milan asked.

"Not yet," said the teacher.

Milan waited some more. Then the teacher said, "Now it is later. Time to go."

Milan held his coin for the library pot. He found the bright red truck book. He sat down and turned the first page.

Jaxson ran to the table. His hands were dirty with mud. "Snack time!" he called. Mama looked at his hands. She shook her head. "Hands first," she said. She pointed to the sink.

Jaxson went to the sink. He turned the cold tap. The water felt cool and smooth. He rubbed the soap. One hand, two hands. Bubbles grew big and white. The mud went down the drain. He watched it swirl away. "Bye, mud," he said.

Now his hands were clean. He ran back to the table. He picked up his apple slice. It crunched in his mouth. Mama smiled. The baby girl in her high chair banged her spoon. "Ba!" she said.

Later Jaxson played in the bath. The water was warm. His rubber duck floated by. After the bath, he put on his soft pajamas. One leg, two legs, all done. He yawned a big yawn. Mama read him a book about a little girl and her dog. Jaxson's eyes closed. The duck sat on the shelf and watched. "Night night, duck," Mama whispered.

Hazel put her teddy bear on the picnic table. "This is my library," she said. She lined up her books in little rows. The animal books sat together. The toy books sat together. The food books sat together.

Rabbit hopped by and stopped. Rabbit wanted a book about animals. Hazel looked at her rows. She went straight to the animal row. There was a book with a bunny on the cover. "Here you go," said Hazel. Rabbit made a happy sound, a little thump on the grass.

Then Hazel heard a small chirp. A bird wanted a book too. Hazel looked and looked. Which row? The bird was an animal. So she patted the animal row. There was a book with a blue bird on it. The bird pecked the cover gently, then flew up with the pages flapping. "Books fly home at my library," said Hazel.

Alice sat in her car seat. Today they were going to Grandma's house. The wheels went round and round on the road.

Alice wanted to see Grandma now. "Are we there yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "We will get there later. First we drive, then we arrive."

Alice looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The car went past, and the cow got small and small. Alice put her finger on the window. "Bye, cow."

Yesterday Alice had packed her small red bag. The bag was heavy with her teddy bear. Mom had helped her lift it into the car. Tomorrow Grandma would make pancakes. But how long was tomorrow?

Alice held up one hand. She counted her fingers. One for today. One for tomorrow. She wanted to count a whole week. "A week has seven days," said Mom. Alice counted. One, two, three, four, five. Her hand ran out of fingers.

"I need more fingers!" Alice said. She looked at her other hand. She opened it wide and counted on. Six, seven. There. A whole week filled two hands.

The car turned a corner. A red gate came into view. Grandma was waving by the door.

"Grandma!" Alice called. "I counted a week with my fingers!"

"Well," said Grandma, "come and tell me all about it."

Rowan wanted to make cookies. Mama mixed the dough in a big round bowl. Rowan got the cookie cutters. One was a circle. One was a square. One was a triangle.

Rowan pressed the circle cutter down. "Look, a circle cookie!" he said. Then he wanted to cut the circle cookie into two little cookies. He looked for a corner to start cutting. He looked and looked. He turned the cookie over. There was no corner anywhere. "Where is the corner?" he said. Mama laughed. "Look again," she said. Rowan ran his finger all around the edge. Round and round and round. No corner, not one.

Rowan picked up the square cookie instead. He felt its corners. One, two, three, four! He cut it from corner to corner. Two triangles fell apart on the table. "I did it!" said Rowan.

Mama put the cookies in the oven. Rowan waited by the closed oven door. He sang a little song while he waited. Then the cookies came out, and there was a small surprise. The circle cookie had puffed up like a little pillow, round on top too. No corners up there either. Rowan took a bite of his triangle. "Best cookies ever," said Mama. Rowan grinned and sang his song again.

Henry put on his blue sweater. He ran to the park with Dad. The red truck was there. Henry wanted to ride it. But a girl was on it now. Henry had to wait. He felt a bit angry. He stomped his foot. Dad said, "We can come back tomorrow." Henry asked, "Where did today go?" Dad said, "After you sleep tonight, today will be called yesterday." Henry thought about that all day. At night he closed his eyes. He slept and slept. Then the sun came up. "It is today again!" said Henry. He ran to the park. The grass was wet. It had rained yesterday. The red truck sat all alone. Henry jumped on and rode round and round. "I waited, and now it is today!" he said. Dad clapped his hands.

Zoey sat at the dinner table. Her father put down a big pot of soup. "It's hot," he said. "I will pour it."

Zoey's little brother Sam sat in his high chair. He saw the soup and smiled. He was excited. He kicked his feet and laughed.

Then Sam grabbed his spoon. The spoon fell on the floor. He reached for it, but it was too far. His face turned sad. Then tears came. Big wet tears ran down his cheeks. When Sam felt sad, he cried.

Zoey looked around the table. She saw her bread. She held it out to Sam. "Do you want some?" she asked.

Sam stopped crying. He took the bread. He took a little bite. "Mmm," he said. Now he was happy again.

"Eat your soup too," said her father. "Careful, it's bumpy with big peas."

Zoey ate her soup. A pea rolled on her tongue. She chased it with her spoon. "Got it!" she said.

Sam laughed and clapped. "Zoey!" he said.

Felix stood in the band room. He held a little drum and two sticks. He wanted to play a song like the big kids.

On the stand there was a paper. It had dots and lines on it. "What are those?" Felix asked. Miss Kay smiled. "Let's find out," she said.

Miss Kay pointed at a dot. She hit the drum one time. Then she pointed at another dot. She hit it two times. Felix watched. The dots were telling her what to play!

Felix looked at the paper. He hit his drum one time, then two times. He waited. He looked again. He hit a slow beat, then a fast beat. "The dots talk to me!" he said.

A bird sat by the window. It sang along. Felix did not get upset when he missed a dot. He just looked again and tried once more. Miss Kay clapped. "Play it again," she said.

Felix hit the drum. The bird sang. The dots went up, and the sounds went up too.

Hudson put on his shoes. Today was his birthday party. Grandma drove him to the bowling alley.

At the door, his friend Milo was crying. "I thought I would get lost," said Milo. "I did not know where to go."

Hudson had an idea. He pulled out his card. "Look," he said. "My mom drew a map on it. It says the party is here. It says three o'clock, too." Milo stopped crying. He looked at the card. The bowling alley was right there on the paper. "Then I am in the safe place," said Milo. "I came to the right spot!"

Milo's dad was with him, and he smiled. The boys ran to the lanes. Hudson picked a little blue ball. He pushed it down the floor. The ball rolled and rolled. Crash! All the pins fell down. Milo clapped his hands.

The friends ate cake at a big table. Grandma lit the candles, and everyone sang. Hudson blew out the candles in one big puff. "Happy birthday, Hudson!" said Milo, with cake on his nose.

Florence ran to the shape table at school. She wanted to make a sun for the class picture. The sun needed one big circle.

She found a big paper circle. Hooray! Then she wanted little circles for the sun's face. She found a tiny button on the craft tray.

Tom looked over. "That button can't be a circle," he said. "The clock on the wall is a circle. Your button is too small."

Florence held the button up high. She traced around it with her finger. Round and round it went. Then she looked at the clock. Round and round that went too.

"Watch this," she said. She pressed the button into the paint. She stamped it on her paper. A small circle appeared! She stamped it again and again.

"The big one is the sun," she said. "The little ones can be birds going to their nest." She stamped small circles across the sky.

Tom grabbed a button too. "I want to pay for my picture," he said, and he glued a button on like a coin. "A circle for money!"

Miss Patel hung both pictures on the safe wall by the window. Florence pointed at her sun. "Big circle, lots of little circles," she said. "They all go round!"

Jules ran into the kitchen. Something smelled good. He used his nose to sniff. "Mama, what is that smell?" Mama was making pancakes. "Use your eyes to see," she said. Jules looked. Round pancakes sat on a plate.

Jules wanted to touch one. "Hot," said Mama. "You must wait." She put one pancake on a cool plate for him. Jules touched it with one finger. It was soft and warm. Mama poured batter into the pan. Jules heard it sizzle. Knock, knock. That was the door. "Daddy is home!" said Jules. He was not late after all.

Jules took a small bite. Yum, sweet! Then he wondered. How did his nose smell the pancakes? He ran to the hallway mirror. He looked at his face. There were two little openings in his nose. He breathed in. His nose moved a tiny bit. One opening, two openings. Both were working!

"How many openings does my nose have?" he asked Mama. He counted in the mirror. "One, two," he said. Mama laughed and put the top pancake on his plate. Jules sniffed it again. Both little openings took in the sweet smell. He took another big bite.

Ibrahim woke up. The sun was in his window. "Time to brush your teeth," said Mama. "We brush in the morning." Ibrahim saw the toothpaste. He squeezed it. It went rip on the brush. He brushed his teeth. They felt clean and good.

Then Ibrahim ate his bread. He drank his milk. One cup, one plate, one sleepy yawn. He played with his blocks. Mama made a warm bath for him. She tested the water with her hand. Ibrahim splashed and laughed. He put on his soft pajamas, one leg, two legs, done.

At last Ibrahim got into bed. He pulled the blanket up. Then he popped back out. "My teeth!" he said. "We brush before bed too!" He ran to the sink. Rip went the paste again. He brushed up and down. Then he ran back to bed. "Good boy," said Mama. She kissed his head and turned off the light.

Oliver sat at the kitchen table. His big sister Poppy poured out buttons. "Let's count them!" said Oliver. "Yes!" said Poppy. She made two rows.

Oliver looked at the rows. One row went all the way across the table. The other row was bunched up in a small pile. "This one has more!" said Oliver. He pointed at the long row.

"Count them," said Poppy. Oliver touched each button in the long row. "One, two, three, four, five." Then he counted the small pile. "One, two, three, four, five."

Oliver jumped up. "Both rows have five!" He pushed the long row close together. He counted again. Still five! He spread the pile out wide. Still five!

Oliver laughed. His soft toy bee sat by the salt. He made the bee hop over both rows. "Five and five!" said the bee, in a funny little voice.

Oliver counted one more time, just to be sure. "Five!"

Paisley wanted a bedtime story about a funny rabbit. But Mama said, "Pick one book from your shelf." Paisley looked and looked. She found a book with a rabbit on the front.

She opened it near the end by mistake. "The rabbit is already asleep," she said. "The story is done!" Mama turned the book around. She went back to the front cover. She opened the first page. The rabbit woke up there and began to play.

"The story starts at the front," said Mama. Paisley tapped the cover. "Who made this up?" she asked. There were words on the front too. Mama put her finger under one name. "This is the author," she said. "She wrote the words."

Paisley traced the letters with her finger. Then she held the book up high. "I found the rabbit lady," she whispered. "Now read, Mama. Start at the front."

Mila packed her little red backpack. She put in her teddy bear, Dot. "We are going camping," said Mama. "First we ride in a big plane."

At the airport, Mila saw a long line. People put their bags on a moving belt. The bags went into a big machine. The machine has a little tunnel, like a cave for bags.

Mila put her backpack on the belt. It slid away. It went into the tunnel. Then it was gone!

"My Dot!" cried Mila. "Where is my Dot?"

Daddy knelt down beside her. "Watch the belt," he said. "Just watch."

Mila watched and watched. Then, pop! Her backpack came out the other end. It slid right down to her. Mila opened the top. Dot was inside, safe and soft.

"Dot went through the machine," said Mila. She hugged Dot tight. "Dot came out the other end!"

The security man at the desk smiled at her. Mila stood tall and proud. She carried her backpack all by herself onto the plane.

Later, at the campsite, Mila put Dot on her pillow. "You went in a machine," she whispered. "And you came out the other end."

Dot sat still, in the tent.

Iris went to Mama's office. She saw a tablet on the big desk. "Can I draw?" she asked. "Yes," said Mama. "First we turn it on." Mama pressed the round button. The screen lit up. Iris tapped it too. The screen woke up again. The tap made it work.

Iris looked at the small pictures on the screen. One little picture had a paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said. Iris drew a green monkey with a long tail. She drew a banana too. Then she was done. She gave the tablet to Mama. Mama put it away in the soft bag. Iris looked at her paper cat next. She wanted to cut it out. "The scissors are sharp," said Mama. "I will cut it for you." Iris watched the paper snip, snip, snip. "Now it can stand up," said Iris.

Victoria had a cold. She sat at the table for breakfast. The sky outside was cloudy. "Sniff, sniff," went Victoria's nose.

Mama gave her warm oatmeal. Victoria took a bite. "Sniff, sniff," went her nose again. She wiped it on her sleeve. Her sleeve got wet and sticky. That did not feel good.

"Let's name what your nose needs," said Mama. "A napkin? No. A towel? No. A tissue? Yes!" Victoria took a tissue from the box. She blew her nose, one big toot. Now her nose was clear.

After breakfast, Victoria sat by the window. She could smell her apple now. She watched the big tree sway. "I hope we can play under it soon," she said. She held the tissue box on her lap, all ready.

Edouard stood in the music room. Miss Rosa played a song on the piano. "Now we clap!" she said. Everyone clapped fast. Everyone clapped slow. Edouard clapped too fast. He clapped when the song was quiet. He clapped when the song was loud. His hands went everywhere!

"Can I learn a short song?" Edouard asked. "One that is not long?" Miss Rosa smiled. "Yes! A nursery rhyme is short. It has rhyming words. My grandpa taught me one when I was little." She sang, "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Edouard listened. The words rhymed. Star and are. High and sky.

"Now clap the steady beat," said Miss Rosa. Clap, clap, clap. Edouard clapped with the beat. He sang the rhyme from memory. His hands felt the beat. His mouth sang the words. "I did it!" he laughed. His friend Ben clapped too. They sang the short song two times. Then three times! "Again!" said Edouard.

Violet got to daycare in the morning. The sun was low and yellow. She put her coat on her hook. She wanted to paint a picture for Grandma. But paint time was later, after snack.

Violet played with blocks. She poured cold water in the sand table. The sand turned dark and sticky. "Look," said her friend Sam. "The water made it wet."

Violet ate her snack. Then the class went outside. The sun was high now. It was hot on her shoulders. After outside time came lunch. After lunch came a nap.

Violet slept on her little mat. When she woke up, she rubbed her eyes. "Is it morning now?" she asked. "Can I paint now?"

Teacher Mia shook her head and smiled. "It is afternoon now, Violet. The morning went by. It is nap-then-play time."

So it was afternoon. The sun was on the other side of the window. Violet sat at the paint table. She painted a big yellow sun.

"That is for Grandma," she said. Grandma would come this afternoon, after daycare. Tomorrow Violet would paint her a moon.

Ryan sat at the little desk at the library. He wanted to write his name all by himself. A kind lady gave him a fat pencil and paper. "Grip it near the point," she said. Ryan held it tight and smiled.

He drew an R first. Then he drew a y, then an a, then an n. But he had started at the right side of the paper. There was no room left. His n squished into a tiny corner. Ryan made a sour face. "Too small!" he said.

He looked at the paper. Then he thought hard. He slid the pencil to the left side. He began again. R, then y, then a, then n. This time every letter fit. His whole name went across the page. Ryan lifted the pencil up high. "Look what I did!" he said. The kind lady clapped.

Ruby came to Grandma's house after a long drive. Grandma was cooking rice. The pot was hot, so Grandma stirred it herself. Ruby watched from her chair.

Soon the food was on the table. Grandma put a warm, fuzzy wrap around Ruby's shoulders. Then they folded their hands. "Bismillah," said Grandma, before her first bite.

Ruby picked up her spoon. She opened her mouth. Then she stopped. She put the spoon down. "Wait!" said Ruby. She folded her little hands. "Bismillah!" she said, loud and proud.

Grandma clapped her hands. "Yes! You said it first!"

Ruby giggled and took a big bite of rice. One grain stuck to her nose. Grandma laughed and wiped it off.

"My turn again," said Ruby. "Bismillah!" She tapped her empty spoon on the bowl.
"Now there is nothing to eat, silly one," said Grandma.
"Then put more rice," said Ruby.

Grayson woke up and saw white outside. Snow! Lots and lots of snow.

"No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day."

Grayson wanted to play with his friend Nia. But first he had to find her. He could not call her. He put on his boots.

He stepped into the snow. His boots made marks. Each step made a print. He looked back and saw his own path.

Then he saw more prints. They were small prints. They went past the big tree. They went up the walk.

"Mom, come see!" said Grayson. "These are not my prints!"

They followed the prints. Step, step, step. The snow felt bumpy under his boots. The prints stopped at a door.

The door opened. It was Nia!

"I came to ask you to play," she said.

Grayson clapped his hands. "Your feet showed me the way!"

Ava sits at the art table. She wants to make a house. She takes a crayon and draws. The roof looks wrong. "My house is lost," she says. She means the shape is lost.

Miss Mia comes close. "Try this," she says. She gives Ava a small block. She gives her little stickers, too.

Ava puts a sticker on the block. One face. She turns the block. Another sticker. Two faces. She keeps turning. Three, four, five, six. Six stickers. Six faces. Each one is a square, like a window.

Ava smiles big. She dips the square face in paint. She presses it on her paper. A square print! She presses it again and again. Squares make a tall house wall.

Then she finds a paper circle. She presses it on top. It looks like a round sun.

"Look," says Ava. "My house came back."

Miss Mia peels the banana skin back for snack time. "Nice square walls," she says.

Ava takes her picture home that day.

Brielle got to school early. The table had pencils and paper. Today she would write her name.

"Make a B first," said Ms. Amy. Brielle gripped the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard. The B looked like a potato.

Then it was time to line up. Brielle ran with her pencil up high. The point waved near Ben's nose. Ben jumped back.

Brielle stopped. She looked at the point. She turned it down by her side. She walked slowly to the rug.

Ms. Amy smiled. "Nice walking," she said.

Brielle went back to the table. She held the pencil with her fingers, not her fist. She made a B. Then an R. "It looks like a real B!" said Ben.

Brielle counted her letters. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." B-R-I-E-L-L-E.

"That is my whole name," said Brielle. "It is not a joke. It is real."

Mohamed wanted a bedtime story. He ran to the shelf and grabbed his book. But it was Dad's old book, the one with funny letters.

Mohamed opened it from the left side. He saw pages with no pictures. He turned one page. Then another. Where were the pictures? He felt dizzy from all the little marks.

"Maybe I opened it the wrong way," he said. He closed the book. Then he opened it from the other side. The first page had a big sun! Under the sun were little marks too.

Dad sat down beside him. "Read with me," said Dad. Dad put his finger at the right side of the page. His finger moved to the left. The marks made words, and the words made the story of a turtle who wanted to grow big.

"Again," said Mohamed. Dad turned the page. His finger started at the right again. Mohamed put his little finger next to Dad's big finger. "My turn," he said.

Jasmine ran to the door. "Park day!" she called. Her mom held up a bottle. "Wait, Jasmine. Sunscreen first." Jasmine stamped her foot. "Why?" she asked. "The sun is so shiny and bright," said Mom. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin." Mom rubbed it on Jasmine's arms. She rubbed it on Jasmine's neck. "Now we can go."

The park was hot and sunny. Jasmine played on the swings. The wind blew her hair. The wind blew the leaves. Big clouds came. Drip, drip, drop. Rain fell! Mom opened an umbrella. Then the rain turned soft and white. "Snow in summer?" asked Jasmine. "No," said Mom. "It is just petals from the tree."

Jasmine picked up a petal. She put it in her pocket to take home. Her friend Ben sat on the bench. His face was red. "I forgot my sunscreen," he said. Jasmine looked at her arms. They were not red. "Come on," she said. "My mom has more. She can rub some on you." Ben smiled and took her hand.

Leah stood in the pool changing room. She pulled on her swim suit all by herself. "Today I will swim," she said. Mum smiled and zipped the bag.

The pool was big and noisy. Leah saw the lifeguard sitting up high in a tall chair. "Why does she sit up there?" Leah wondered. Then Leah got in at the little steps. She held a red noodle. She kicked her feet. Splash, splash! The water was warm.

Then her hands let go. The red noodle floated away. Leah could not reach it. Before she could call out, a whistle blew. Tweet! The lifeguard slid down and reached with a long pole. The noodle came back to Leah's hands. "You saw me from up there!" Leah said. The lifeguard nodded and climbed back up. The room went quiet again. Leah held her noodle tight and kicked on and on.

Hudson stood in the school gym. He had a red beanbag in his hand. A hoop lay on the floor far away.

Hudson threw the beanbag overhand. The beanbag flew past the hoop. It landed with a soft sound on the mat.

"Can I try again?" Hudson asked.

"Yes," said Miss Kim. "Watch me. I will show you a new way."

Miss Kim held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop.

"Your arm starts low," said Miss Kim. "Swing it forward and up."

Hudson held his beanbag down low. He swung his arm forward and up. The beanbag sailed through the air. It landed near the hoop.

"Close!" said his friend Mila. "Try again."

Hudson tried again. Swing, up, drop. The beanbag fell right into the hoop.

"I did it!" said Hudson.

Then Miss Kim rolled a big blue ball to him. Hudson put out both hands. The ball bumped his chest and fell down. It was a messy try. He ran after the ball.

The ball came again. This time Hudson held both hands out wide. The ball landed in his arms. He hugged it tight.

"Nice catch," said Mila.

Hudson laughed and rolled the ball back. "Your turn," he said.

Leah went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about animals. The books were all mixed up on the cart. "Which ones are animal books?" she wondered.

A boy named Sam was there too. He had a pile of picture cards. Sam put all the red cards in one pile. Then Leah had an idea. She took the red cards and made a new pile. She put the big red cards together. She put the small red cards together. "Look, Sam! Red cards, big and small!" Sam clapped his hands. Then he patted his toy lion on its soft nose. "Can we sort my lion too?" he asked.

The librarian smiled and brought three bins. Leah put toy books in one bin. She put food books in one bin. She put animal books in one bin. Then Leah found a funny book. It had a picture of an ugly green monster eating soup. Leah laughed. "Dad, look at this one!" Dad read it to her twice. On the way home, Leah held her new book tight and said, "Books can go in piles too."

Bennett went to Grandma's house. A new baby sister was coming. Grandma said, "We need to get ready."

Bennett found a big box. He cut the tape with safety scissors. Grandma held the box steady. Inside were diapers. Small ones. So many diapers.

"Why so many?" Bennett asked.

"We will see," said Grandma.

Then baby Rose came home. Bennett watched. Rose drank her milk. Then Rose made a wet diaper. Grandma changed it. One diaper in the basket.

Rose drank more milk. Another wet diaper. Two diapers in the basket.

"Again?" said Bennett.

"Again," said Grandma. "She is too little for the toilet."

Bennett counted the diapers. One, two, three, four. The basket got full. Bennett felt a little sad. The diapers were going too fast.

Then Grandma gave him a job. "Draw a picture for Rose," she said. Bennett took his pencil. He drew a big happy baby. He drew a big stack of diapers too.

Rose looked at the picture. Rose waved her small hand.

"Hello, Rose," said Bennett. "I will count your diapers every day."

Josephine wanted to build a big bed for her teddy. She found a big box at daycare. She pulled it. The box was too heavy. It did not move. "Oh no," said Josephine.

Her friend Sam ran over. He ran fast. Then he walked slow, so he would not bump her. Sam pulled too. Still the box did not move. It was heavy, heavy, heavy.

Miss Ruby came with a small white pillow. It was light. Josephine picked it up. Up, up, easy! She put the pillow in a small box. "A bed!" she said. She gave teddy a kiss. On the wall was a picture of a fire truck, big and red. Josephine yawned a big yawn. "Teddy is slow to sleep," she said. "Shh."

Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. She was going to get a fuzzy new toothbrush. But first, the nurse said Grace could pick a sticker.

"I want the ice cream sticker," said Grace. She reached out her hands. Then she saw them. There was glitter glue on her fingers from the waiting room.

"The glitter can hide in the little lines on your hands," said the nurse. "Let's wash it off."

At the little sink, Grace scrubbed fast. The glitter stayed. She scrubbed again, fast fast fast. Still it stayed.

The nurse began to sing. "Happy birthday to you." Grace sang too. They sang it all the way through, and Grace kept scrubbing.

Grace looked down. Her hands were shiny and clean. "The song made my washing long," she said.

The nurse smiled and gave her the sticker. Grace held it up to the light.

Evan was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a big red rug with letters on it. Evan wanted to find every letter he knew.

"Look, Grandma! A B!" he said. Then he saw another letter. It looked the same. It looked different. It was shy, hiding its face.

"Grandma, this word says bog!" Evan read. Then he laughed. "Bog! That is a funny word!"

Grandma laughed too. Evan got down on his knees. He looked very close. One round part faced left. One round part faced right.

"It is not bog," Evan said. "It is dog! The dog lives next door!"

Grandma found a feather by the door. Evan used the feather to point. "B goes this way," he said. "D goes that way!"

He pointed at the letters again and again. "This way! That way! This way!" Then Evan jumped up.

"Grandma, I can read dog! Let's find more words!"

Sarah ran into the library. "Books!" she said. "So many books!"

Today was story day. Miss Kim put out big cards. One card had a picture of animals. One had a picture of toys. One had a picture of foods.

"Put each card in its group," said Miss Kim.

Sarah picked up a cow. "Animals!" She put it down. Then she found a ball. "Toys!"

Then she held up an apple. "Foods!" she said.

Ben shook his head. "Fruits!" he said.

"You are both right," said Miss Kim. "Put it in two spots."

Sarah bent down. She set the apple with the foods. Then she picked it up again. She set it with the fruits too.

The apple sat in two places at once. Sarah laughed and clapped her hands.

Max sat at Grandma's kitchen table. He wanted to write his name all by himself. His brother could write his name already. But Max was too young for big kid school, and his letters came out wobbly.

"How do the letters get straight?" Max asked.

Grandma gave him a paper. It had dotted letters on it. The dots made the shape of M-A-X. Grandma held the pencil in his hand. She showed him where his fingers should go.

Max pushed the pencil along the dots. The pencil made a line. The line went right over the dots! He traced the M. He traced the A. He traced the X. Each dotted letter turned into a dark, solid letter.

"Look what I made!" Max said.

Grandma put the paper up on the fridge to dry. Max ran to get more paper. "Can I do my name again?" he asked. "One more time, then two more times!"

Anna wanted to find her toy robot. It was lost somewhere in the house. She looked with her eyes. She listened with her ears. She heard a little beep. Was it under the bed? Yes! The robot was there, covered in dust.

Anna pulled the robot out. Some dust flew up. She blinked and blinked. The dust did not get in her eyes. Her eyelashes caught it. She touched her eyelashes with her fingers. "They are like tiny gates," she thought. "Where does the dust go if I blink?" It went away. Her eyes stayed clean.

Then Anna smelled cookies with her nose. Daddy had baked them. She tasted one. It was sweet and warm. She touched the warm plate, very carefully. "Found you, robot!" she said. She hugged him tight. The robot beeped a happy beep.

Ivy sat on the grass by Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone was warm and dry in the sun. Mama set out a picnic blanket. "We eat lunch here," Mama said. "Grandpa Ben liked picnics."

Ivy was hungry. She grabbed a bread roll right away. Mama held up her hand. "Wait," she said. "First we say our blessing." Ivy put the roll down. She did not know the blessing yet. That was her problem.

Mama folded her hands. "One, we thank the sun. Two, we thank the rain. Three, we thank the farmers." Then Mama began to eat. Ivy looked at her roll. She thought about the farmers. They grew the wheat. That was one more thing to thank.

"I want to say it too," said Ivy. She folded her hands. "One, thank you, sun. Two, thank you, rain. Three, thank you, farmers." Then she took a big breath. "Four, thank you, Grandpa Ben." Mama's eyes went shiny and glad. She gave Ivy a big smile.

Ivy bit into her roll. It tasted good and warm. A little breeze moved the grass near the stone. It felt like a hello. Ivy waved back. "Bye, Grandpa Ben," she said. "Same picnic next week?"

Matteo put on his new shoes. He tapped each foot, one, then the other. "First day of school," said Mama. Matteo held her hand very tight.

The classroom was big. It was full of toys and small chairs. Matteo did not know anyone. He hid behind Mama's coat. A lady with a red sweater came over. "Hello, Matteo," she said. "My name is Miss Jo. I am the teacher." She knelt down and smiled. She showed Matteo a box of blocks. She helped him stack one, then two, then three.

Mama sat on a little chair and waited. Matteo looked at her. Then he looked at Miss Jo. He took one small step. "Hello, Miss Jo," he said, very quiet. Miss Jo clapped her hands. Matteo stacked another block. It went up, up, up, and stayed.

Zoe sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a magic dragon. The dragon would be red, like fire.

Zoe picked up her brush. She dipped it in the red paint. She painted the dragon's long tail. Then she wanted yellow wings. She dipped the brush in the yellow pot.

The yellow came out all pink and muddy. Zoe frowned. Her yellow wings looked wrong. The red had jumped into the yellow!

Zoe put her brush in the water cup. She swished it round and round. The water turned pink. Then she counted to three, like a game. She dipped the brush in the yellow again.

Now the yellow was bright as the sun. Zoe painted big yellow wings. Then she swished the brush again, and dipped it in the blue pot. Yellow and blue touched on the paper.

A green spot grew. It looked like a leaf from a magic tree. Zoe clapped her hands.

Tom leaned over from the next seat. "Can I have a turn with the magic water?"

"Yes," said Zoe, in her polite dragon-queen voice. "Swish first. Then the colours stay clean."

Tom swished his brush. His paint stayed bright too. Together they painted a green forest for the dragon to fly over.

Sophie ran onto the green grass. Her team wore red shirts. Grandpa sat on the gray bench by the field. He waved at her.

The game began. Sophie got the ball. She kicked it hard. The ball rolled and rolled. But it went the wrong way. It went toward her own net. The other kids ran after it.

"Uh oh," said Sophie. "Which net is mine?" She looked and looked. The red team was at the far end. "That one," she said. She turned around.

She ran fast. Her friend Ben stopped the ball. He passed it to her. Sophie kicked with her foot. The ball went into the other net. The red team cheered.

"Sophie scored!" said Ben. Grandpa clapped and clapped. Sophie smiled a big smile. She did not cry. She hugged the ball.

"Good kick," said Grandpa.

"Again!" said Sophie. And she ran back to the game.

Raphael was playing house at daycare. He put his teddy bear in a small chair. He gave the teddy a pretend drink from a tiny cup.

Then his friend Mia came over. She was holding her doll. Oh no! The doll fell on the floor. Mia began to cry. "Dolly fell down," she said.

Raphael picked up the doll. He looked at it. Was the doll hurt? He touched the doll's arm. It was soft, like a thick sock. The doll did not cry. The doll could not cry at all. Dolls are just toys. But wait, maybe it could feel better anyway?

Raphael gave the doll a big hug. "There, there," he said, like his mom said to him. Then he rocked the doll in his arms. Would the doll feel better now? He could not know. But he could pretend!

Mia stopped crying. She watched Raphael hug her doll. "Can I hug dolly too?" she asked. Raphael gave the doll back. Mia held it close and patted its little sock hat. "Dolly is all better," she said.

Raphael smiled. He went back to his teddy bear. He covered the teddy with a small blanket. "Night night, teddy," he said. The teddy lay very still. It was just pretending to sleep, just like the doll was just pretending to feel better. Raphael patted the teddy's soft head.

Ivy ran to the swing. "Papa, when is Saturday?" she asked. "Saturday is the day we fly your big red kite," said Papa.

"Not soon enough," said Ivy. "Count the days with me," said Papa. He held up his hand. "Today is Sunday. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." His fingers stopped. "Seven days make one week. Saturday is day seven."

Ivy jumped off the swing. She picked up a stick. "One, two, three," she drew lines in the soft dirt. "Four, five, six, seven." Seven little lines lay in the dirt. Each night, one line would go away.

"Can I make the lines go fast?" asked Ivy. Papa laughed. "Time goes on its own. But you can help it feel quick."

So they counted the slide steps. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!" Then Ivy was careful going down, so she would not spill her juice cup on the way.

Each day, one line went away. Sunday, Monday, Tuesday. On Saturday morning, one last little line was left. Ivy wiped it with her shoe. "Zero!" she said. "Zero days left!"

Papa held the kite up high. The summer wind pulled it. "One, two, three!" said Papa, and he ran. Ivy ran too, in the bright blue sky's light, chasing the wiggly red tail.

Lily loved her school bag. It was big. Her friend Ben had a small bag. "One bag, two bags," they said.

At school, they played outside. Lily ran fast. Ben walked slow. The sun was hot. The water from the tap was cold. Lily washed her hands. A snail sat by the wall. "Slimy," said Lily. She touched it, very gently.

After lunch, the class had nap time. Lily closed her eyes. She slept and slept. Then she woke up. The room was dark. "It's morning!" Lily began to shout. "Time to play!"

Miss Maya came over. She opened the curtain a little. Lily looked out. The sky was black. One star, two stars, three stars. The sun was not there.

"It is still night," said Lily, quietly. "Night is dark. Day is light."

Miss Maya smiled. Lily went back to her mat. She closed her eyes. Outside, the stars stayed. One star, two stars, three.

Milan went to the park with his dad. He saw a red strawberry in the picnic basket. "Can I eat it?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. Milan held it up. It smelled so sweet. His nose knew that smell right away.

Then Milan had a funny idea. What if he held his nose shut? He pinched his nose with his fingers. He took a big bite. "Yuck!" he said. "It tastes plain now!" The strawberry tasted like nothing much at all. He let go of his nose. He took another bite. The sweet taste came back! "Dad, my nose helps me taste!" he said.

Dad laughed. "How funny," he said. Milan looked at the ducks on the pond. He listened to them quack. He touched the soft grass with his toes. "What a lucky day," said Milan. He ate one more strawberry, nose wide open.

Maria went to her music teacher's studio. Her teacher, Miss Ana, had a big drum there. "You can build a beat," said Miss Ana. Maria tapped the drum. Boom, boom! The sound was big like a lion. Maria tapped again. Boom, boom, boom!

Then Maria's mom and her friend Sam came in to listen. Maria played her drum song. Boom, boom, boom! The room felt hot from all the clapping hands. Everyone clapped and clapped. Maria just stood there. Miss Ana smiled and bowed down low. Maria watched her. Then Maria bowed down low too, just like that.

Everyone clapped again. "Yay, Maria!" said Sam. Maria drummed one more time. Boom! Then she bowed. "Again!" said Sam. Maria laughed and bowed again.

Emily wanted her bedtime book about the bunny. She found it on her shelf. She opened the back cover by mistake. The pages went the wrong way.

"Try the front," said Dad. Emily turned the book around. She opened the front cover. Now the bunny came first. On the first page she saw small black marks. "What are those?" she asked.

"Those are words," said Dad. "They say the story." Dad read them out loud. The marks made the bunny story!

Emily loved the curly letters and the pictures. "Who drew the bunny?" she asked.

Dad pointed to a name on the first page. "This person drew the pictures. This person is the illustrator." The name was Kate.

Emily held the book up to the air. "Thank you, Kate!" she said.

Ivy sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her teddy was missing from her bag. "Where did he go?" she asked. She looked with her eyes at the floor. She listened with her ears. She heard voices and a phone. No teddy.

The nurse smiled. "Maybe he fell in the exam room," she said. They walked in together. The room was dark. Ivy could not see much. "Too dark," she said. The nurse reached up and switched on the lamp. Click. Now the room was bright. Ivy saw her teddy under the chair. "There he is!" She ran and picked him up.

The doctor came in. "I hear you found your teddy," she said. "You have a good team." Ivy held teddy close. He smelled like soap. She kissed his soft ear. "You taste like breakfast," she said. The doctor laughed and laughed.

Beatrice sat in a big chair at the mall. The hairdresser, Miss Jo, put a cape on her. Snip, snip went the scissors. Beatrice watched the little hairs fall down.

"I want to see my hair," said Beatrice. She turned her head one way. She could see the front. She turned her head the other way. She still could not see the back. Her neck felt funny and itchy. She rubbed it with her hand.

"Wait right there," said Miss Jo. She picked up a small mirror. She held it up behind Beatrice's head. Now Beatrice could see the big mirror in front and the little mirror too. There was the back of her hair, short and neat.

"Oh! I see it!" said Beatrice. She stuck out her finger and touched the mirror. The girl in the mirror touched back. Beatrice giggled and giggled. "Hi, back hair!" she said.

Chloe went to the store with her dad. She held his hand in the parking lot. "Look at all the cars," she said. They were red, blue, yellow and green.

Chloe wanted a toy pig from the store. But first they had to cross the street. They stopped at the curb. The light was red. "The red car is stopping," said Chloe. Every car stood still. Then the light turned green. The cars rolled away. Dad gave her hand a little swing. "Green means the cars go," said Chloe. They waited for a new red light, and then no cars came, and they walked across.

Inside the store, Chloe found her pig. It was pink and heavy. She carried it in both arms. Dad smiled and opened the door for her. "Beep, beep," said Chloe, and rolled her pig down the walk like a little green car.

Jacob ran to the big playground. The sun felt hot on his nose. He wanted to ride down the slide. But a girl was banging a drum near the slide. Bang, bang, bang! It was so loud.

"The drum is loud," said Jacob. "My ears want quiet." The girl, Mia, stopped. She tapped the drum softly. Tap, tap. Now it was quiet. Jacob laughed. "Loud and quiet! The drum can do both?"

"Yes," said Mia. "Want to try?" Jacob tapped the drum. First loud, then quiet. His hands made it loud. His hands made it quiet. "I did it!" he said.

Then he rode down the slide, fast fast fast. He rolled to the small swing and went slow. On the way home, Dad gave Jacob a gift. It was a tiny drum, smelly like new shoes. Jacob tapped it. Just one little quiet tap. "Shh," he whispered. "The baby is napping."

Leah stood by the classroom door and looked at the big alphabet chart. Her teacher, Mrs. Park, was writing letters on the board.

"Leah, can you find the letter S?" asked Mrs. Park.

Leah found it. "S goes sss," she said, wiggling like a snake. Ben laughed next to her.

Then Leah looked at the chart again. There were so many letters. She wanted to count them. She touched A. "One," she said. She touched B. "Two." She kept going, all the way down the row.

"Twenty-six!" she shouted. "Twenty-six letters, all in a row!"

"That many?" said Ben. "Count again. I don't believe it."

Leah counted again. She did not slip up. "Twenty-six," she said again.

So Mrs. Park had an idea. "Let's find a letter for each friend," she said. "When I say your name, say the first sound."

"Ben," said Mrs. Park.

"Buh, buh, Ben!" said Ben.

"Leah," said Mrs. Park.

"Luh, luh, Leah!" said Leah. Then she ran to the chart and put her finger on L.

"Hard to believe we all fit," said Ben, counting the kids.

The bell rang. Leah waved at the chart on her way out. "Bye, twenty-six letters," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Sara ran to the park with her bunny. "We will swing high!" she said. But when she got off the swing, bunny was gone. Sara looked in the sand. No bunny. She looked by the slide. No bunny. A big dog barked near the bench. Sara looked there too. Still no bunny.

Then she saw a small wooden box. A sign said Lost and Found. Sara peeked inside. There was a red mitten. There was a thin blue scarf. There was a green cup. One, two, three things, and then, something soft. "Bunny!" Sara shouted. A kind man in a green shirt smiled. "Someone found him and put him in the box," he said. Sara hugged bunny tight. "Park, box, bunny," she sang all the way home. "Found you, found you, found you!"

Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She had blocks of many shapes. She found a round block. It rolled away. "Too wobbly!" she said. That block was a circle, and circles roll.

She found a block with three sides. "A triangle!" It made a fine roof, pointy at the top. Then she found a long block with four sides. A rectangle! Perfect for the wall.

She looked for one more square block. Her friend Ben pointed at a tilted block. "Look, a new shape!" he said. "It has a corner pointing up!"

Lillian turned the block back down flat. It was the same square! She laughed. "Silly block. You are still a square!"

She stacked the square at the bottom. The house stood tall. She tucked the snake inside. "Home at last!" said Lillian.

James ran into the writing club with his big sister's pet rabbit soft toy under his arm. He sat down fast. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

Miss Ana gave him a pencil. She showed him how to hold it. "Pinch it like this," she said. James pinched the pencil. He drew a J, then an A. He drew an S, then an M. Then he stopped and looked. "J-A-S-M-E? That looks funny," he said. His friend Lily slid the name card over to him. James looked at the card. The letters were J-A-M-E-S. He erased two letters. He wrote them back the right way. "Now it says James!" he shouted. "It popped into place!"

Miss Ana clapped. James held up his paper. "Look, rabbit!" he said. "Your friend has a full name on my page." Then he started on a new paper right away. "I'm making another one," he said.

Kinsley sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump on the road. "Are we there now?" she asked. "Not yet," said Mom. "We will get there later."

Kinsley looked out the window. A cow stood by a fence. The cow chewed grass. Yesterday Kinsley saw a cow too. That was yesterday. Today she saw a new cow. Tomorrow they would drive home again.

"Is it later yet?" asked Kinsley. Mom pointed to the clock in the car. "Look at the clock," she said. "The clock shows what time it is. When the little hand gets to the five, we will be there." Kinsley watched the clock. The little hand moved slow, slow, slow. It got to the four. Then it got near the five.

The car stopped. "Here we are," said Mom. "Now it is later!" Kinsley climbed down from her seat. Grandma held out a juicy red apple. "For you," said Grandma. Kinsley took a big bite. Then she found her book in her bag and sat on the porch step. The clock had said five, and now it was five. "We came at five," said Kinsley, turning a page.

Aubrey sat at the dinner table. She had peas on her plate. She wanted more peas, but she did not know how to ask.

Daddy held up one finger. "You are this many," he said. Aubrey peeked at his finger. Then she held up three little fingers. "I am three!" she said. Daddy clapped. "Yes! You are three."

Mommy said, "Let's count your peas." Aubrey pointed. "One, two, three, four, five." Mommy smiled. "You counted five peas. Now you can have more." Daddy gave her five more peas.

Aubrey counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten peas! She ate them one by one.

Then Aubrey felt upset. Her cup was empty. "Uh oh," she said. Mommy poured in milk from the big cup. Aubrey took a big sip.

"I am three," said Aubrey. She held up her fingers to the window, where the river shone far away. "Three, like that!"

Wyatt wanted grapes. "You can have three," said Mom. Wyatt looked at the bowl. The grapes were small.

He picked one, two, three small grapes. Then he saw a big grape. It was fat and round. "Maybe a big grape counts as two," he thought. He put the big grape in his hand too.

Mom shook her head with a smile. "Three is three," she said. Wyatt put one small grape back. One, two, three. The big grape stayed. A little bug crawled on the table. Wyatt watched it while he ate.

The big grape was sweet and cold. Juice ran down his chin. Mom gave him a napkin. "One, two, three," Wyatt said again. He counted his grapes, and every time, three meant three. "More please," he said.

Snow fell past the window while Lucy played. "Look, a blue crayon," she said. Her brother Ben shook his head. "That one is too dark. That is not blue." Lucy held it up to her doll's dress. The dress was blue too, but a light blue, like the snow was almost white. "It is blue," said Lucy. "It is just dark blue."

"Let's ask the crayons," said Ben. They dumped them all out. Lucy picked the blue ones. "One, two, three, four, five!" She lined them up in a row. The first was very light. The last was very dark, deep as night. "They are all blue," said Lucy. "Light blue, dark blue, blue, blue, blue."

Ben tapped the darkest one. "Okay, it is blue. But it is sleepy blue." Lucy laughed. She drew a big deep blue sky. Then she added tiny white snow dots with her other hand.

Penelope loved water day at daycare. Teacher Mia filled the little tub outside. Penelope splashed and splashed. Soon her arms were all wet. Drip, drip, drip went her fingers.

Tommy ran past her, dripping too. He ran to the sand box. Sand stuck all over his wet legs. "Oh no," said Tommy. "Sand on me!"

Penelope looked at the towel rack. She took a big blue towel. She rubbed her arms. Rub, rub. The towel made her arms dry and warm. Then she went to play, dry and happy.

Tommy came back. "Towel, please," he said. Teacher Mia smiled. "Kind Penelope can help you." Penelope patted Tommy's legs with the towel. The sand fell off, all clean.

"Now let's get dressed," said Teacher Mia. Penelope put on her dry socks. "Water day is the best day," said Tommy. Penelope laughed and wiggled her warm toes.

Aurora was three, and today was her first trip to the dentist. She sat in a big chair. It went up when the dentist pushed a button. A little wheel on the chair spun round and round. "Whee!" said Aurora.

The dentist had a surprise. "Pick a toothbrush," she said. "You get your very own." There was a pink one and a green one. Aurora took the pink one. But a young boy next to her grabbed it too. He held it tight.

"That is mine!" said Aurora. "Is it yours?" she asked him. "No," he said. "Mine is green. I took the wrong one." He put the pink one back. He took the green one instead. Now Aurora had pink, and he had green. "Two toothbrushes, two kids," said Aurora. "One for each!" The dentist laughed. "Let me see that smile," she said. Aurora opened her mouth wide, like a baby bird.
