Sofia wanted to play the senses game. Mama said, "Tell me each sense. Then find it in the house."

Sofia began with eyes. "I see with my eyes," she said. She looked out the window. She saw the moon, big and white.

"I hear with my ears." Then a dog barked outside. Sofia laughed. Her ears heard it fast.

"I smell with my nose." She sniffed the bread. "Mmm," she said.

"I taste with my tongue." Mama gave her a tiny taste of jam. It was sweet.

Then Sofia stopped. "What is the last one?" she asked. She felt a little worried she would forget.

Mama put a pine cone in her hand. Sofia touched it with her fingertips. "Ooh, it is bumpy," she said. She touched her soft blanket. Then her smooth cup.

"I feel with my fingers," she said. "My skin feels it all!"

Mama clapped. Sofia touched Mama's warm hand. "This feels the best," she said.

Leah wants to play rocket ship at the playground. But her rocket is not ready yet. It has a wobbly ladder and a sticky wheel.

Leah cleans the sticky wheel with her sleeve. Now the wheel spins fast. Papa holds the wobbly ladder and fixes it tight. "Thank you, Papa," says Leah.

Now the rocket is ready. A boy named Sam wants to fly too. Leah and Sam make a line to climb in. First Leah, then Sam. "We need a countdown," says Sam. "Count down from ten!"

Leah counts, "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Leah jumps up high. Sam jumps up high too. They fly to the moon together.

Sam holds out his hand. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten stars!" he says. Leah looks up and counts them too. She is so happy.

Then Leah counts down again. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one." Sam jumps. "Blast off!" they shout, and run to the swings.

Charlie ran to the little table at school. Today he would write his name! Ms. Rose gave him a fat pencil. "Hold it like this," she said. Charlie gripped it tight. He pressed down hard. The pencil slid off the paper. The C came out all wobbly. "Yucky," Charlie said. "My C looks like a squiggle."

Ms. Rose smiled. "Try sorting your letters first," she said. She gave him two roads of paper. One road was for straight letters. One road was for curvy letters. Charlie picked up the C. It had a big curve. He put it on the curvy road. He picked up the L. Straight lines, top to bottom! He put it on the straight road. A, H, L, straight. C and R, curvy. "Two curvy, three straight!" he said.

Now Charlie knew his letters. He lifted his pencil and went slow. Straight lines for L, easy peasy. The C took a big round curve, round like a ball. One letter, two letters, three letters, four, five, six, seven. "Charlie!" he shouted. "I did it! My name is on the paper!" He lifted the paper up high. "Look, Ms. Rose! Look at my road of letters!"

Hailey sat in the cafe with her mama. Mama gave her a pencil and a paper napkin. "Can you write your name?" asked Mama.

Hailey grabbed the pencil in her fist. She pushed hard. The letters came out big and wobbly. An H looked like a ugly little squiggle. "Mine looks wrong," said Hailey. Her lip went down, almost ready to cry.

Mama sat close. She kissed the top of Hailey's head. Then she showed her hand. She pinched the pencil with her thumb and her first finger. The pencil rested on her middle finger. Hailey tried it. Pinch and rest. Pinch and rest. The pencil felt light in her hand now.

Hailey drew an H. It stood up tall. Then an A, then an I. The pencil made neat little lines. "Look, Mama!" said Hailey. Her whole name sat on the napkin, letter by letter, small and clear.

Paisley walks to the bookmobile with her mom. The big van is blue and white. It smells like paper and sunshine inside. Paisley wants a book about ponies. She wants one so, so much.

She finds a pony book on a low shelf. The cover feels rough. She hugs it tight. "This one," she says. "I want this one."

A man at the small desk smiles. "You can have your very own library card today," he says. He hands Paisley a little card. It is orange. Her name is on it. Paisley holds it with two hands.

Then the man scans the book. He scans her card too. "All done," he says. "Take the book home."

Paisley gasps. "Home? The book comes home with me?" She jumps up and down. "The card makes it mine for now. The card makes it mine!"

Mom laughs. "Yes. Your card means you can borrow it. We will read it tonight."

Paisley carries the book all the way. She holds it against her chest. It is a good feeling, warm like a hug.

At bedtime, Mom reads the pony book. Paisley pets the rough cover, soft and slow. "Good night, ponies," she says. "See you for three more stories tomorrow."

Emile wanted to find the dog in the book. He opened the book from the left. The pages went the wrong way. They would not turn.

His friend Noa came over. She held up a small flag with blue stripes. "This book is Hebrew," she said. "It opens from the other side."

Emile looked at the back of the book. He tried it. The cover opened! The thick pages turned one by one.

Noa pointed to the little letters. "We start here," she said. She pointed to the right side of the page. Emile put his finger there too.

They slid their fingers to the left. The letters made words. The words made the story. And there, on the last page, was a big brown dog.

"Woof!" said Emile.

Mason lost his monkey. His soft, spotted monkey was gone. He looked at Grandma's house. He looked under the bed. No monkey. He looked in the big chair. No monkey. He looked in the toy box. No monkey.

"Where can he be?" Mason asked. Grandma said, "Did you take him outside?" Mason had played by the gate. He ran to look. There was his monkey, sitting by the fence! But then a bus stopped. A kind driver held up the monkey. "Who lost this?" she asked. She looked at the tag. It said Mason. "This tag has your name," she said. "Now I know he is yours."

Grandma helped Mason write his name on the tag. Mason read it out loud. "M, A, S, O, N." His name was on his monkey. Grandma said, "Now everyone will know." Mason hugged his monkey tight. "Home with me," he whispered.

Milo got to school with a red apple in his bag. He waved to his teacher, a kind woman with a loose paint smock. "Today we paint," she said. "We paint after nap time."

Milo loved to paint cats. He thought about his cat all morning. He built with blocks. He ate his apple. Then it was time to rest.

Milo slept on his little blue mat. When he woke up, the light felt soft and yellow. "It is morning," he said. "I missed the painting!"

His teacher shook her head and smiled. "No, Milo. Look outside." The sun was low in the sky. "It was morning before your nap. Now it is afternoon."

Milo looked out the window. The sun sat behind the trees. It was afternoon, and the painting table was open.

"Today is still today!" said Milo. He paid close attention to his brush. He painted a big orange cat, all the way until the light grew dim.

Sarah went to the store with Dad. Today was Monday. "Pancakes are on Saturday," said Dad. Sarah wanted pancakes now. "How many days is that?" she asked. Dad said, "Count with me." Sarah held up her little hand. They tapped each finger together. "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday." Sarah looked at her fingers. Six days! Then she saw it. One more finger was still down. "A week has seven days," she said to herself, counting all her fingers. Seven felt like a lot of days.

Sarah and Dad walked down the store aisle. "Guess what we need," said Dad. Sarah pointed at the bread. "Yes! And look, these crackers are little triangles." Sarah picked up a triangle cracker box. "It looks like a little roof," she said. A lady walked by with a small dog in her arms. "What a cute dog," said Sarah. The dog wagged its tail.

At home, Sarah helped Dad put the bread away. She stood on her step stool, far from the hot stove. "Dad, is Saturday soon?" she asked. Dad said, "Sleep six times, and it is here." Sarah smiled. She held up her fingers and counted them again. Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday. "I can wait," said Sarah. Dad kissed the top of her head. "Saturday pancakes for my girl," he said.

Charles went to book club with his mama. There was a big rug and a basket of books. "A, B, C," said Miss Ana. "Letter B says buh. Letter D says duh."

Charles picked a book about a dog. But he read it his own way. "The bog says woof!" he said. He giggled and giggled.

"Is it a bog or a dog?" asked Miss Ana.

Charles looked. He counted the round parts. "One round part," he said. He turned his finger around and around. Then he saw it. "The b goes this way. The d goes that way."

Miss Ana laughed. "You did it, Charles."

Charles patted the picture. "It is a dog. A dog is an animal. A bog is not."

"Good thinking," said Miss Ana. "Now what is this word?"

It was "bed." Charles looked closely. Round parts, one this way, one that way. "Bed!" he said. "The dog can dry off on the bed. He is itchy and wet."

"That is a silly dog," laughed Miss Ana.

Charles turned the page. "D is for dog," he said. "Woof, woof!"

Mateo sat in the car seat. He held his soft blue bunny. Then the car went over a bump. Bunny jumped out of his hands. Bunny was gone.

"Bunny!" said Mateo. He looked down. He looked under the seat. It was too dark. He could not see anything at all. "Oh no," he said. "Bunny is alone down there."

Daddy stopped the car at the store. The store would sell bread and milk. Daddy looked back. "What is wrong?" he asked.

"I lost Bunny," said Mateo. "It is dark under the seat. I cannot see."

Daddy reached into the glove box. He took out a little flashlight. He clicked it on. The light was bright and yellow. "Here," said Daddy. "Try this."

Mateo pointed the flashlight under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. The light made it bright. And there was Bunny! Bunny was sitting by a tissue and a cracker.

"Bunny!" Mateo shouted. He reached down. He grabbed Bunny's soft ear. He pulled him up fast. "I found you!" he said. He hugged Bunny tight. Bunny's fur touched Mateo's hair.

Daddy laughed. "Good helper, that light," he said.

Mateo held Bunny and the flashlight together. "Now we can find anything," said Mateo. "Anything at all!" He clicked the light on and off. On and off. "Let's go, Daddy. Let's go buy bread!"

Arya went to the library with Dad. She wanted the book about the salty sea. "It lives on shelf five," said the librarian. Arya looked at her fingers. One, two, three, four, five. Then she saw the shelves. Each shelf had a number on top.

She found a shelf with a big 5. "Five!" she said. She counted her fingers again. One, two, three, four, five. The same five! The salty sea book sat right there. She pulled it out. "I found it!" she said. Dad laughed. "You clever counter."

On the way out, Arya counted the steps. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. The door let them out into the sun.

"Ten steps," said Arya. "Ten big steps!" Dad said, "Let's count them again on the way home." Arya held her book tight and began. One, two, three.

Sadie sat in her car seat. She had a bag of crackers. Her dad drove the car. "Big truck!" said Sadie. "Cool truck," said Dad.

Then they stopped. Grandma was in the car too. Grandma looked hungry. Sadie held out her bag. "Crackers? Please take one," said Sadie. Grandma took a cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," said Grandma. Sadie opened her mouth. Then she closed it. What could she say back? She thought and thought. The car went slow. The car went fast.

Then Dad handed Grandma his hat. "Thank you," said Grandma. "You're welcome," said Dad. Sadie sat up tall. Now she knew the words. Grandma took one more cracker. "Thank you, Sadie," said Grandma. "You're welcome," said Sadie. Grandma smiled big. "You're welcome," said Sadie again. Dad read the road sign out loud. "Home soon," he said. Sadie hugged her cracker bag. "You're welcome," she whispered, one more time.

Mason wanted to hold the red balloon. It was Daddy's balloon from the party.

Mason grabbed for it. The string slipped away. Daddy shook his head. "Try again," Daddy said.

Mason thought hard. He remembered his lion book. The little lion wanted a turn with the ball. The little lion said, "May I have a turn?" Then he got the ball.

Mason took a big breath. "May I have a turn?" he asked. Daddy smiled wide. "Yes, you may!" Daddy put the string in Mason's hand.

The balloon bumped the ceiling. Mason laughed and laughed. He held the string with both hands. The balloon went up, then down, then up again.

"Thank you, Daddy," Mason said. Daddy gave him a hug. "You asked so nicely," Daddy said. "That was very polite."

Mason walked slowly with the balloon. The lion book sat on the shelf. "Night night, lion," Mason whispered. The balloon floated above his head.

Billie ran to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on her face. She went to the little slide first. Then she saw the red truck at the far end.

"I want that truck," said Billie. She ran past the swings. She ran past the sandbox. She ran to the fence.

Billie looked back. She could not see Dad. The swings were in the way. She stood very still.

Then she heard Dad call, "Billie! Where are you?" His voice came from the swings. Billie ran back past the sandbox. She ran to the big tree by the swings. Dad was right there.

"There you are," said Dad. He held her hand. "Stay where I can see you."

They walked to the red truck together. The truck sat in the sun. Dad touched it first. "It is hot," he said. "We will find a shady truck."

They found a blue truck in the shade. It felt cool. Billie pushed it down the slide. It went fast. Dad clapped his hands.

On the way home they passed Billie's school. "My school," said Billie. "I sort blocks there. Red blocks go here. Blue blocks go there."

A lazy cat lay by the school door. It blinked one eye at Billie. Billie waved. The cat purred and went back to sleep.

Weston ran to the dress-up corner at daycare. He wanted to wear the firefighter hat. But the big basket was all mixed up.

"A jumble," said Miss Dana. She sat down next to him. "Let's look inside."

Weston dug in. He found a sock. He held it up. "A sock! Socks are not toys. Socks are clothes." He dropped it into the clothes pile. Then he found a bear. "A bear is a toy." He put the bear in the toy bin. He laughed at the silly sock sitting with the bear.

Next he found a shirt. Clothes. A banana from the play kitchen. That was food. He made a food pile too. Soon the basket was empty.

"Where is my hat?" asked Weston. Miss Dana pointed. The hat was on the shelf, next to a triangle block. Weston grabbed it. He put it on his head.

The phone rang, ding ding. It was Baby Sam, crying. His hands were sticky from jam. Weston ran over with a cloth. "I help you," he said. He wiped Sam's hands.

Sam smiled. Weston smiled too. Then he set the phone on the table and put a plate of pretend bananas next to it. "Snack time," he said.

Raphael was at the community centre. The sun came in the big window. He sat on the floor with his friend Mia.

"I have more blocks," said Mia.
"No, I have more," said Raphael.

They both wanted the red blocks. Miss Jo said, "Try lining them up."

So they did. One block here. One block there. One across from one. They counted as they went. "One, two, three, four, five." Raphael's row was longer. His row had blocks left over.

"See? You have more," said Mia. She looked a little sad.

Raphael pushed two blocks across the floor. "Now we both have five," he said.

Then something fell. It was an ice cube, and it began to melt on the warm floor.

"Who put an ice cube there?" asked Raphael.

Mia laughed. "It was me. It was a surprise. My hands were hot!"

Raphael touched the wet spot. The ice cube had turned to water. Not broken. Just water.

"Let's get ten blocks," said Raphael. "Then we can line them all up."

"Ten blocks, one long row," said Mia. "Let's count."

"One, two, three," said Raphael, and they counted on and on.

Harper sat in a big blue chair at the dentist. She held her gray toy mouse tight. "It will be okay," said Mama.

The dentist came in. "Hello, Harper," she said. Harper looked at her hands. They were blue. "Why are your hands blue?" Harper asked. "Do you have blue skin?"

The dentist smiled. She pinched one blue finger. Then she pulled it off. Underneath was a pink finger. Harper's eyes went wide. It was not skin. It was a glove.

"Can I see?" asked Harper. The dentist showed her. One glove, two gloves, both blue. She put them on again, snap, snap. Now her hands were clean for looking at teeth. Harper let go of her mouse.

"Open wide," said the dentist. Harper opened her mouth. The dentist counted out loud. "One tooth, two teeth, three teeth." She counted all the way to twenty. Then Harper got a small mirror. She looked at her own teeth and smiled.

Avery went to the store with Mama. The store had bright lights and big shelves. Avery saw a red apple. She wanted the red apple. She grabbed for it.

Mama shook her head. She held Avery's hand. Avery looked at the apple. Then she said, "Apple, please." Mama smiled and put the apple in the cart. Avery held the apple all the way to the bread aisle.

A little boy was there too. He reached for the bread. His mama shook her head. The little boy stopped. He said, "Bread, please." His mama gave him the bread. Avery watched. He got the bread, just like she got the apple.

At the checkout, they waited in line. First the lady in front went. Then it was Avery's turn. Avery put the apple on the belt. "Please," she said to the man at the register. The man smiled a big smile. He put the apple in the bag. Avery carried the bag to the car. "My apple," she said. "I asked so nice."

Henry went with Dad to the hospital. Mom had a new baby. The baby was so small and young.

The baby began to cry. "Why is he crying?" Henry asked. Mom said, "You can try to find out."

Henry looked at the baby. He waited. The baby kept crying. Henry saw the baby's mouth open and close. "Maybe he is hungry," Henry said. Mom gave the baby milk. The baby drank and stopped crying.

Later the baby cried again. Henry looked again. "Not milk this time," he said. He touched the baby's soft blanket. It had slid down. Henry pulled the blanket up. The baby stopped crying and went to sleep.

Henry gave the baby a kiss on his head. Henry's shoes still had sand from the park. He wiggled his toes and whispered, "Crying means you need me."

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet book. She wanted to know every letter. Mom sat next to her on the soft cushion.

"Let's count them," said Mom. Brielle pointed at each letter. "A, B, C, D." She went on and on. Her sock slipped off one foot, but she kept pointing. "W, X, Y, Z."

"I counted all the way to twenty-six!" said Brielle. Her eyes got big. She counted again to be sure. Twenty-six again!

Then she made the letter sounds. "B says buh. B is for book!" She hugged the book.

"Now let's clean up," said Mom. Brielle put on her sock. She picked up her toys. "A is for away," she said, pushing the truck away from the nook. "A says ah!"

Mom laughed. "You did it, Brielle."

Brielle smiled and traced the letters with her finger, all twenty-six.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. He had a big pencil. He wanted to write his name. "I can do it," he said. Mom sat next to him. Jackson held the pencil in his fist. "Try two fingers on top," said Mom. Jackson tried. The pencil felt better now.

Jackson began at the right side of the paper. He made a J. Then an A. Then the pencil ran out of room. No space for the rest! "Oh no," said Jackson. "The letters won't fit." He had to miss some letters out. His name looked wrong. Mom turned the paper around. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side. Jackson started at the left. J, A, C, K. The letters went across the page. There was room for all of them! "Jackson!" he read. Then the door opened. It was Dad, home early, with a wet umbrella. "Is that your name?" Dad asked. Jackson held up the paper. "I wrote it all by myself."

Madeline went to the park with Dad. She wanted to paint a card for Grandma. She saw red flowers. She saw blue flowers. She saw yellow flowers too. "Grandma loves pink best," said Madeline. But she had no pink paint.

She sat at the little park table. Dad put out the paints. One cup was red. One cup was white. One cup was green. Madeline frowned at the red cup. "No pink," she said.

Then she had an idea. She dipped her brush in the red paint. She put a red dot on the card. She dipped her brush in the white paint. She stirred the red dot around and around. The red dot turned light. It turned soft. It turned pink! "Pink!" said Madeline. "I made pink!"

She painted one pink flower. Then two pink flowers. Then three pink flowers. She painted green stems. She painted a blue sky. She painted a yellow sun.

Then Dad pushed her on the swing. The swing went high. Madeline held the card tight. "Pink flowers for Grandma!" she called. Dad smiled and gave the swing one more little push.

Lennon wanted to draw a big cloud. She could not find paper. Then she saw the library tablet on its stand.

Lennon tapped the top button. The screen lit up. On the screen were small pictures. One small picture looked like a paintbrush. Lennon tapped it. Tap! The drawing app opened, all by itself. She drew a fat white cloud. She drew a yellow sun too.

A boy came by. He looked sad. He wanted a turn. Lennon finished her cloud and showed him the paintbrush picture. "Tap this," she said. He tapped it and started to draw. Lennon pushed the button to make the screen dark. She put the tablet back on the stand, just where it belonged.

Alexander dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped in a seed and patted it flat. "Grow, little seed," he said.

Every morning he ran to the backyard swing. He swung high, then jumped off and looked at his garden. Nothing was there. Just dirt. Day after day, just dirt.

A bird landed nearby. It stuck out its tongue and chirped at the dry ground. Alexander touched the dirt. It was dry and crumbly, like crackers.

He ran inside. "Dad, my seeds will not grow!" he called.

Dad came out with the watering can. "Try this," he said. Alexander tipped it over the dirt. Water dripped down, dark and cool. He watered the spot every day after that.

One morning, something small and green stood in the dirt. It had two tiny leaves, new and soft. Alexander knelt down very close. "Hello," he whispered, and gave it a little more water.

Norah sat at the paint table at school. She wanted to paint a pumpkin. She looked for orange paint. There was no orange. "Oh no," she said. "How can I paint my pumpkin orange?"

Her friend Milo sat next to her. Milo was painting with red paint. He had yellow paint too. He poured some red and some yellow into his cup. He stirred them with his brush. The paint turned orange! The paint smelled a little stinky, but Norah did not mind.

"Can I try that?" Norah asked. "Yes," said Milo. She put red in her cup. She put yellow in too. She stirred and stirred. Orange! She painted her pumpkin round and bright.

Teacher Ann came to look. "What a big orange pumpkin," she said. "Can I pay you with a sticker?" Norah grinned. "Yes, please." She stuck the sticker right on her smock.

Athena went to the store with Grandma. Yesterday they had no milk at home. Today they needed to buy some. Athena held Grandma's hand in the big store.

Athena saw a pink balloon by the door. It floated up high. "Can I have one?" she asked. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we get the milk." Athena made a sad face. Soon felt like a long, long time.

They walked past the bread. They walked past the apples. Athena helped put the milk in the cart. Then they found cheese. The cart got full. It was not full yesterday. It was full now.

Then Grandma stopped walking. She pointed at the balloons. "Now," she said. Athena picked a pink one. She did not have to wait forever. Soon was just a little while.

At the bus stop, Athena held her balloon tight. The bus came down the street. "Today was a good day," said Grandma. Athena smiled. "Tomorrow can we come back?" she asked. Grandma laughed and hugged her. The bus doors opened with a big whoosh, and Athena stepped up, holding her pink string high.

Asher stood at the school gate. His new backpack sat on his back. It was very full. It was very heavy. His legs felt slow.

Asher wanted to run to the door. But the bag pulled him back. He could not walk fast. He looked in the bag. He saw his toy truck. He saw his toy bear. He saw three more toys.

Asher sat on the wall by the gate. He took the toys out, one by one. His dad held them in his hands. The bag got light. The bag got small on Asher's back.

A girl came to the gate. Her bag was big and round. It looked heavy too. She stopped walking. "My bag is too full," she said. Asher smiled. He showed her how to open his bag. She took out her toy farm animals. Her bag got light too.

Then Asher ran to the door. The wind blew the gate shut. It almost hit a small boy. Asher put out his hand. The gate was slippery from the rain. It slid past his hand anyway. The teacher caught it just in time.

"Now we can wave to our dads," said the girl. They turned around. They waved big waves. And Asher walked into school, quick as a hop.

Paint day was here at last. Charlotte ran to the art table. She wanted to paint a big rainbow for her mom. But there were only three paint pots. Red, yellow, and blue. Charlotte frowned. "Where are the other colours?" she asked. Her friend Tom, a boy with paint on his nose, said, "That is all we have today." Charlotte looked at her rainbow picture. It needed green and orange. She looked at the paint pots again. The teacher had left the pots open on the table. Charlotte dipped her brush in the blue pot. Then she dipped it in the yellow pot. The brush made a new colour on the paper. It was green! "Blue and yellow make green," Charlotte whispered. She tried red and yellow next. The brush made orange. Her rainbow grew and grew. Tom painted beside her, making purple with red and blue. Charlotte held up her rainbow. "Can I paint another one?" she asked. The teacher smiled and nodded. Outside, a dog barked at the sunny window. Charlotte picked up her clean brush.

Ibrahim sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a house. He looked for a good shape. He found paper squares. He found paper circles too. Teacher Amna sat next to him. She had her brown spoon. She was mixing paint with it.

"Can a house be round?" Ibrahim asked. "No," he said. He put the circle aside. He picked up a square. He glued it down for the house walls. Then he looked for a roof. He held up a triangle. "How many corners does it have?" he asked. He touched each one. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners and three sides. The triangle sat on top of the square. The house had a roof.

Teacher Amna had her snack. Her sandwich was cut into triangles. Ibrahim pointed at a piece. "One, two, three," he said. Three corners again. She smiled and gave him a piece. He took a big bite.

Next to him, Sara dropped her brush. Paint was going to spill. "Teacher Amna!" Ibrahim yelled. She caught the cup with her brown spoon. Nothing spilled. Sara gave Ibrahim a paper rectangle. "For your door," she said. He glued it on. "One, two, three," he said, touching the roof corners one more time.

Jasper sat on his bed. He put on his sock. He put on his shoe. He wanted to go to Mila's house now. "Mila now," he said. Mama shook her head. "Not now, Jasper. It is night. We go tomorrow." Jasper was sorry. His face went sad. "But now," he said. "First we sleep," said Mama. "Then it is tomorrow. Then we go." Jasper got one book. Then he got his bear. Then he got his blanket. One, two, three. Mama read the book. Jasper's eyes closed. He slept all night. Then the sun came up. Light sat on his blanket. "Morning!" said Jasper. "It is today!" He ran to find Mama. "The sleeping is done. Now it is tomorrow. Now we go to Mila's house!" Mama laughed. She took his hand. "Yes. Today we go. You keep your shoes on so we are ready." Jasper looked down at his shoes. He had never taken them off.
